GIve eare, the worthy, heare what Fame proclaimes. More than you underſtand, my hot Inquiſitors, I came from Saturne. You are neere the right. Indeed, he is Time it ſelfe, and his name KRONOS, The Time hath ſent me with my Trumpe to ſummon All ſorts of perſons worthy, to the view Of ſome great ſpectacle he meanes to night, T'exhibite; and with all ſolemnitie. Not ſo laviſh. Who's this? Away, I know thee not, wretched Impoſtor, Creature of glory, Mountebanke of witte, Selfe-loving Braggart, Fame doth ſound no trumpet To ſuch vaine, empty fooles: 'Tis Infamy Thou ſerv'ſt, and follow'ſt, ſcorne of all the Muſes, Goe revell with thine ignorant admirers, Let worthy names alone. How now! what's here? Is hell broke looſe? The next? What are this paire? Yes. What a confederacie of Folly is here! I envie not the 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . 'Twill prove but deifying of a Pompion. You might imagine ſo, I never promis'd it. A comely licence. They that cenſure thoſe They ought to reverence, meet they that old curſe, To beg their bread, and feele eternall Winter. Ther's difference 'twixt liberty, and licence. Any thing. Agree among your ſelves, And what it is you'ld have, I'le anſwer you. Theſe are meere Monſters. You doe abuſe the Time. Theſe are fit freedomes For lawleſſe Prentices, on a Shrovetueſday, When they compell the Time to ſerve their riot. For drunken Wakes, and ſtrutting Beare-baytings, That ſavour only of their owne abuſes. I'le fit you, though the Time faintly permit it. Why now they are kindly us'd, like ſuch ſpectators, That know not what they would have. Commonly, The curious are ill natur'd, and like flies, Seeke Times corrupted parts to blow upon: But may the ſound ones live with fame, and honour, Free from the moleſtation of theſe Inſects: Who being fled, Fame now perſues her errand. For you, great King, to whom the Time doth owe All his reſpects, and reverence, behold How Saturne, urged at requeſt of Love, Prepares the object to the place to night. Within yond' darkneſſe, Venus hath found out That Hecate (as ſhe is Queene of ſhades) Keepes certaine glories of the Time obſcur'd, There, for her ſelfe alone to gaze upon, As ſhe did once the faire Endimion. Theſe, Time hath promis'd at Loves ſuit to free, As being fitter to adorne the age, By you reſtor'd on earth, moſt like his owne: And fill this world of beautie here, your Court. To which his bountie, ſee, how men prepare To fit their votes below, and thronging come With longing paſſion to enjoy th'effect! Harke, it is Love begins to Time. Expect.
What? what? I'ſt worth our eares? And hearken. However, goe you on, let us alone. Saturne, what is he? One of their Gods, and ea • es up his owne children. As Cincinnatus Was from the plough, to be Dictator. Where men might doe, and talke all that they liſt. And ſubjects of their Soveraigne. It was a brave time that! And heare the paſſages, and ſeverall humors Of men, as they are ſwayd by their affections: Some grumbling, and ſome mutining, ſome ſcoffing, Some pleas'd, ſome pyning, at all theſe we laughing. And my eares tingle, would it would come forth: This roome will not receive it. 'Tis Chronomaſtix, the brave Satyre, And promiſeth all libertie. Talke what we liſt. Rare! how he talkes in verſe, juſt as he writes! Who feaſts his Muſe with claret wine, and oyſters, Goes as long as an Elephant: That kicks at Time already, A quondam Juſtice, that of late Hath beene diſcarded out o'the pack o'the peace, For ſome lewd levitie he holds in capite, But conſtantly loves him. In dayes of yore, He us'd to give the charge out of his poems, He carries him about him, in his pocket, As Philip's Sonne did Homer, in a casket, And cries, O happy Man, to the wrong party, Meaning the Poet, where he meant the ſubject: For the whole City. This falls upon you For your neglect. You promis'd us, we ſhould have any thing. Or State. We doe it in Pauls. Or let's have all the people in an uprore, None knowing, why, or to what end: and in The midd'ſt of all, ſtart up an old mad woman Preaching of patience. And all diſputing of all things they know not, And all together by the eares o'the ſudden, No, never agree. I, or unreaſonable. And a great noyſe. Wee only hunt for novelty, not truth.
Or eyes? We come to ſpie. It may be. We may ſpie out, that, which you never mean't. Hath beene oft call'd from it, To be their Lord of miſrule. Yes. We need no interpreter, on, what of Time? His dayes of feaſt, and libertie agen. Slaves of their lords. This will be better: I ſpie it comming, peace. All the impoſtures, The prodigies, diſeaſes, and diſtempers, The knaveries of the Time, we ſhall ſee all now. My foure eies itch for it. That which the Time is preſently to ſhew us. Yes Fame muſt know him, all the Town admires him. We know, Sir. But the Time's now come about. We ſhall doe what we liſt. You'l ſee. That he ha's favourers, Fame, and great ones too. That unctuous Bounty, is the Boſſe of Belinſgate, She labours, and lies in of his inventions, And is no ſooner foald, but will neigh ſulphure: The ragged raſcalls? Meere rogues, you'ld thinke them rogues, but they are friends, One is his Printer in diſguiſe, and keepes His preſſe in a hollow tree, where to conceale him, He workes by glow-worme light, the Moone's too open. The other zealous ragge is the Compoſitor, Who in an angle, where the ants inhabite, (The emblem's of his labours) will ſit curl'd Whole dayes, and nights, and worke his eyes out for him. This Man of warre, i'the rere, He is both Trumpet And Champion to his Muſe. Now Fame, how like you this? And theſe will deifie him, to deſpite you. What gambols? what deviſes? what new ſports? Pox, then 'tis nothing. I had now a fancie We might have talk'd o'the King. Cenſur'd the Counſell, e're they cenſure us. No, the Man I'the Moone daunce a Corranto, his buſh At's backe, a fire; and his dogge piping Lachrimae. What? And talking of all men they never heard of, And, when the matter is at hotteſt, then All fall aſleepe. O, that we ſhall never doe. Or impoſſible. To little, or no purpoſe. But ſee, there be no cauſe, as you will anſwer it. Why, if not thoſe, then ſomething to make ſport.
Or noſes? For we are curious, Fame: indeed, the Curious. And ſmell out. And noſe the thing you ſent not. Firſt, whence come you? Some Proteſtant I warrant you, a Time-ſerver, As Fame her ſelfe is. How! Saturne! Chronos! and the Time it ſelfe! You're found: inough. A notable old Pagan! A Fencer, and do's travell with a ſith Inſtead of a long-ſword. O, we ſhall have his Saturnalia. The ſervants of their maſters! I have it here, here, ſtrong, the ſweat of it, And the confuſion (which I love) I noſe it, It tickles mee. That's the feare. The gentleman-like Satyre, cares for no body, His fore-head tip't with bayes, doe you not know him? Nay licence. And cenſure whom we liſt, and how we liſt. Growes big with Satyre; Ha's a male- poem in her belly now, Big as a colt, Strange arguments of love! There is a Schoolemaſter Is turning all his workes too, into Latine, To pure Satyricke Latine; makes his Boyes To learne him; calls him the times Juvenal; Hangs all his Schoole with his ſharpe ſentences; And o're the Execution place hath painted Time whipt, for terror to the Infantery. H'as him by roat, recites him at the tables, Where he doth governe; ſweares him into name, Upon his word, and ſword, for the ſole youth Dares make profeſſion of Poetick truth, Now militant amongſt us: To th'incredulous, That dagger is an article he uſes, To rivet his reſpect into their pates, And make them faithful. Fame, you'l find you'ave wrongd him. He ſcornes you, and defies you, H'as got a Fame on's owne, as well as a Faction. Well, what is that the Time will now exhibite? That Time would give us all we could imagine. Or all the World. Yes, and in all the tavernes! Why if it be not that, let it be this then (For ſince you grant us freedome, we will hold it,) Let's have the giddy world turn'd the heeles upward, And ſing a rare blacke Sanctus, on his head, Of all things out of order. No, no, I'ld ha' this. That could be monſtrous: Enough, I meane. A Babel of wild humours. Not upon what. Something that is unlawfull. Let 't be uncivill enough, you hit us right. And if there be ſome miſchiefe, 'twill become it. I, all the better.
What? what? my friends, will not this roome receive?
The Time? Lo I the man, that hate the time That is, that love it not; and (though in ryme, I here doe ſpeake it) with this whipp you ſee, Doe laſh the Time, and am myſelfe laſh-free. If you would ſee Time quake and ſhake, but name us, It is for that, we are both belov'd, and famous. Then I will looke on Time, and love the ſame, And drop my whip: who's this! my Miſtris! Fame! The lady whom I honour, and adore! What lucke had I not to ſee her before! Pardon me, Madam, more than moſt accurſt, That did not ſpie your Ladiſhip at firſt, T'have giv'n the ſtoop, and to ſalute the skirts Of her, to whom all Ladies elſe are flirts! It is for you, I revell ſo in rime, Deare Miſtris, not for hope I have the Time Will grow the better by it. To ſerve Fame Is all my end, and get my ſelfe a name. O, you the Curious, Breath you to ſee a paſſage ſo injurious, Done with deſpight, and carried with ſuch tumor 'Gainſt me, that am ſo much the friend of rumor? (I would ſay Fame? ) whoſe Muſe hath rid in rapture On a ſoft ambling verſe to every capture, From the ſtrong guard, to the weake childe that reades me, And wonder both of him that loves, or dread's me! Who with the laſh of my immortall pen Have ſcourg'd all ſorts of vices, and of men! Am I rewarded, thus? have I, I ſay, From Envies ſelfe torne praiſe, and bayes away, With which my glorious front, and word at large, Triumphs in print at my admirers charge. When have I walk't the ſtreets, but happy he That had the finger firſt to point at mee, Prentice, or Journeyman! The ſhop doth know it! The unletter'd Clarke! major and minor Poet! The Sempſter hath ſate ſtill as I paſs'd by, And dropt her needle! Fiſh-wives ſtaid their cry ▪ The Boy with buttons, and the Basket wench! To vent their wares into my workes do trench! A pudding-wife that would deſpiſe the Times, Hath utter'd frequent pen'worths, through my rimes, And, with them, div'd into the Chamber-maid, And ſhe unto her Lady hath convay'd The ſeaſon'd morſels, who hath ſent me penſions, To cheriſh, and to heighten my inventions. Well, Fame ſhall know it yet, I have my faction, And friends about me, though it pleaſe detraction, To doe me this affront. Come forth that love me, And now, or never, ſpight of Fame, approve me.
Beſide, that it is done for Love, It is a worke, great Time, will prove Thy honour, as mens hopes above. The night could not theſe glories miſſe, Good Time, I hope, is ta'ne with this. By like her troope ſhee hath begun to miſſe.
If Love be pleaſed, ſo am I: For Time could never yet deny What Love did aske, if Love knew why. You ſhall not long expect: with eaſe The things come forth, are borne to pleaſs: Looke, have you ſeene ſuch lights as theſe? If Time were not, I'am ſure Love is. Betweene us it ſhall be no ſtrife: For now 'tis Love, gives Time his life. The wiſh is crown'd, as ſoone as made. Who's that deſcends? Diana? Let's meet, and queſtion what her errand is. Chaſt Dians purpoſe we doe now conceive, And yeeld thereto.
Shee knew, and hath expreſt it now. And ſo doth every publike vow That heard her why, and waites thy how. Theſe, theſe muſt ſure ſome wonders bee! 1 Their very number, how it takes! 2 What harmony their preſence makes! 3 How they inflame the place! Let Time then ſo with Love conſpire, as ſtraight be ſent into the court A little Cupid, arm'd with fire, Attended by a jocund Sport, To breed delight, and a deſire of being delighted, in the nobler ſort. And CVPID conquers, e're he doth invade. His victories of lighteſt trouble prove. For there is never labour, where is Love. Yes. All Votes doe in one circle move.
O, what a glory 'tis to ſee Mens wiſhes, Time, and Love agree What griefe, or envie had it beene, That theſe, and ſuch had not beene ſeene, But ſtill obſcur'd in ſhade! Who are the glories of the Time, Of youth, and feature too, the prime, And for the light were made! The Courtly ſtrife is done, it ſhould appeare, Betweene the Youths, and Beauties of the yeare, Wee hope that now theſe lights will know their ſpheare, And ſtrive hereafter to ſhine ever here: Like brighteſt Planets, ſtill to move In th'eye of Time, and orbes of Love.
Now they are neerer ſeene, and viewd; For whom could Love have better ſu'd? Or Time have done the grace? Turne Hunters then, agen. Hunting, it is the nobleſt exerciſe, Makes men laborious, active, wiſe, Brings health, and doth the ſpirits delight, It help's the hearing, and the ſight: It teacheth arts that never ſlip The memory, good horſmanſhip, Search, ſharpneſſe, courage, and defence, And chaſeth all ill habits thence. Turne Hunters then, agen, But not of men. Follow his ample; And juſt example, That hates all chace of malice, and of bloud: And ſtudies only wayes of good, To keepe ſoft Peace in breath. Man ſhould not hunt Mankind to death, But ſtrike the enemies of Man; Kill vices if you can: They are your wildeſt beaſts. And when they thickeſt fall, you make the Gods true feaſts.
Take breath awhile, young Blouds, to bring Your forces up, whilſt we goe ſing Freſh charges, to the Beauties here. Or quit the field. My Lords, the Honors of the Crowne, Put off your ſowreneſſe, doe not frown • , Bid cares depart, and buſineſſe hence: A little, for the Time diſpence. The words of Sport, my Lords, and courſe. Your Ladyes yet, will not thinke worſe Of Love for this: they ſhall command My Bow, my Quiver, and my Hand. I ſee the Beauty, that you ſo report. Arme, arme then all. And try his fate. A joyning, but of feet, and hands. Is all the Time, and Love commands.
Or, if they charge you, doe not feare, Though they be better arm'd then you: It is but ſtanding the firſt view, And then they yeeld. Nay, that they'l never doe. They'l rather fall upon the place, Then ſuffer ſuch diſgrace. You are but Men at beſt, they ſay, And they from thoſe ne're ran away. Sir, doubt him more of ſome ſurpriſe Vpon your ſelfe. He hath his eyes. You are the nobleſt object here, And 'tis for you alone I feare: For here are Ladyes, that would give A brave reward, to make Love live Well, all his life, for ſuch a draught. And therefore, looke to every ſhaft, The Wags a Deacon in his craft. Truſt nothing that the Boy lets fall, My Lords, he hath plots upon you all. A Penſioner unto your wives, To keepe you inuxorious gives, And ſo your ſenſe to faſcinate, To make you quit all thought of ſtate, His amorous queſtions to debate. But, heare his Logicke, he will prove There is no buſineſſe, but to be in love. What, here to ſtand and kill the Flies? Alas, thy ſervice they deſpiſe. One Beauty here, hath in her eyes, More ſhafts then from thy bow o're flew, Or that poore quiver knew. Theſe Dames, They need not Love's, they have Natures flames: Cupid, you muſt not point in Court; Where live ſo many of a ſort. Of Harmony theſe learn'd their ſpeech, The Graces did them footing teach, And, at the old Idalian bralls, They daunc'd your Mother downe. Shee calls. Young blouds come on, And charge: Let every man take one. Theſe are faire warres. And will be carried without ſcarres. Or if you doe their gloves off-ſtrip. Or taſte the Nectar of the lip: See, ſo you temper your deſires, For kiſſes, that yee ſucke not fires.
You, Sir, that are the Lord of Time, Receive it not as any crime 'Gainſt Majeſty, that Love and Sport Tonight have entred in your Court.
Hippolitus, Hippolitus. Shee. Be ready you, or Cephalus, To waite on me. Your Goddeſſe hath beene wrong'd to night, By Loves report unto the Time. And it is. I call'd theſe Youth's forth; in their bloud; and prime (Out of the honour, th •• I bore their parts) To make them fitter ſo to ſerve the Time By labour, riding, and thoſe ancient arts, That firſt enabled men unto the warres, And furniſh'd Heaven with ſo many Starres: And ſo may theſe doe, if the Time give leave.
Diana? Wee ever be. The injury, it ſelfe will right, Which only Fame hath made a crime. For Time is wiſe, And hath his eares as perfect as his eyes.
Shee will prevent thee, Saturne, not t' ••• uſ • Her-ſelfe unto thee, rather to complaine That thou and Venus both ſhould ſo abuſe The name of Dian, as to entertaine A thought, that ſhe had purpoſe to defraud The Time, of any glories that nere his: To doe Time honour rather, and applaud His worth, hath beene her ſtudy. As Perſeus, Caſtor, Pollux, and the reſt, Who were of Hunters firſt, of Men the beſt; Whoſe ſhades doe yet remaine within yond' groves, Themſelves there ſporting with their nobler loves:
